synopsis: NeRF learns scene color and density with a neural network to render new viewpoints; the booklet treats it as both a scene-reconstruction method and a learned sensor-model approach [f12925, f3813, f4483]. Reconstruction requires multi-camera logs with accurate poses and GPU compute, optionally using lidar, and offers an alternative to explicit geometry conversion [f4226, f3992]. Log-based neural re-simulation supports closed-loop-like evaluation near the recorded trajectory, but artifacts occur at 1–4 m offsets, height changes degrade results more than sideways shifts, and large viewpoint changes limit testing of new sensor mounting positions [f5722, f5724, f3706, f5723]. Industry preference for 3DGS reflects NeRF’s editing and labeling limitations, yet the cited XLD results found NeRF-based EmerNeRF and UC-NeRF more robust than the 3DGS variant PVG at 4 m offsets [f3878, f4329]. SplatAD at CVPR 2025 claims roughly tenfold faster rendering than NeRF methods; its cited NeRF baselines render 9.7–28.2 megapixels per second after 0.9–2.6 hours of training [f4945, f4946]. For heavy off-road validation, the principal evidence gap is that log-based neural re-simulation has very low off-road maturity and the cited evidence is on-road only [f5725].
